Exactors
eg-ZAK-torz
noun (plural)
From the Latin exigere, to drive out, demand, or require — ex, out, and agere, to drive. An exactor is one who demands payment by force: a tax-farmer, driver, or oppressor who extracts what is owed and more.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs once, in one of the most beautiful promises in Isaiah: “For brass I will bring gold, and for iron I will bring silver, and for wood brass, and for stones iron: I will also make thy officers peace, and thine exactors righteousness” (Isa 60:17). The verse works by a series of upgrades — every material replaced by one of greater worth, brass for wood, gold for brass — and then, having established the pattern, Isaiah applies it to government. The officers shall be peace and the exactors righteousness. He does not say the exactors will be abolished; he says they will be transformed into the very thing they usually destroy. That is a remarkable promise, because the exactor is the figure everyone under an ancient empire feared: the man with authority to take, whose visit meant loss. Isaiah announces a government whose collectors are righteousness itself. The following verse completes the picture: “Violence shall no more be heard in thy land, wasting nor destruction within thy borders; but thou shalt call thy walls Salvation, and thy gates Praise” (Isa 60:18). Not merely peaceful walls but walls named Salvation; not merely open gates but gates called Praise. This is not the abolition of order but its healing — authority restored to what God made it for.

Webster 1828 Definition

Those who demand payment by force — tax-gatherers, drivers, oppressors; in Isa 60:17, the officers whom God promises to transform into righteousness itself.

expand to see more

EXACTOR, n. One who exacts; an officer who collects tribute, taxes, or customs with rigour.

An extortioner; one who compels another to pay more than is due.

From the Latin exigere, to drive out, to demand, from ex and agere, to drive.

Isa 60:17: thine exactors righteousness — the office transformed, not abolished.

The Hebrew is elsewhere rendered taskmaster and oppressor.

Key Scripture

Isa 60:17 — "For brass I will bring gold, and for iron I will bring silver, and for wood brass, and for stones iron: I will also make thy officers peace, and thine exactors righteousness."

Isa 60:18 — "Violence shall no more be heard in thy land, wasting nor destruction within thy borders; but thou shalt call thy walls Salvation, and thy gates Praise."

Isa 60:19 — "The sun shall be no more thy light by day; neither for brightness shall the moon give light unto thee: but the LORD shall be unto thee an everlasting light, and thy God thy glory."

Rev 21:23 — "And the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof."

Modern Corruption

Hope for public life swings between abolishing authority and idolising it, where Isaiah promises neither anarchy nor a strong man but offices healed into peace and righteousness.

expand to see more

The corruption runs in two directions, and Isaiah rebukes both. On one side is the utopian instinct that identifies authority itself as the problem, so that the good future is imagined as a world without officers, taxes, or magistrates. On the other is the reflex that idolises office — the strong ruler who will set matters right, before whom criticism becomes disloyalty. Isa 60:17 grants neither wish. The officers remain and the exactors remain; what changes is what they are. Government is not treated as an evil to be escaped nor as a saviour to be trusted, but as a good thing currently corrupted, which God intends to heal.

Recover the plain sense: authority is God’s ordinance and its abuse is the corruption of something originally good. The magistrate is the minister of God to thee for good; that is Paul’s judgment about a Roman empire that would shortly kill him. So the Christian neither despises office nor worships it, but prays for kings and all that are in authority, obeys where he lawfully may, and looks for the day when the collector at the door is righteousness. And notice where Isaiah’s chapter ends up, because the promise is finally not political at all: the sun shall be no more thy light by day, but the LORD shall be unto thee an everlasting light (Isa 60:19) — a sentence John takes up over the city that has no need of the sun, for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin exigere, to drive out or demand — the forceful collector; promised in Isaiah to be transformed into righteousness.

expand to see more

Exactors — Latin ex + agere, to drive out, to demand.

One who collects tribute with rigour; a taskmaster or oppressor.

Isa 60:17 upgrades every material: wood to brass, brass to gold.

Then applies the pattern to office: officers peace, exactors righteousness.

Isa 60:18: walls called Salvation, and gates called Praise.

Usage

"The exactors are not abolished but transformed — office healed, not removed."

"Isaiah’s hope is neither anarchy nor a strong man."

"The chapter ends with God Himself as the everlasting light (Isa 60:19)."
